name: Onboarding page
description: The screen that tracks a deployment being configured: every task that has to be finished before a document can be raised, grouped, with what is done, what is blocked and on what, who owns each one, and what the page becomes once it is finished.
when_to_use: The first weeks of a deployment, where the company, the plants, the financial year, the numbering series, the tax defaults, the chart of accounts, the item and vendor masters and the opening balances all have to exist before a single purchase order can be raised, and somebody has to be able to see how far that has got. The line against form-page — and specifically its wizard variant — is who owns the clock. A wizard owns the user until it finishes: one record, one sitting, one Save, and the steps are sequential because step 3 needs step 2's answer. This is none of those. The tasks take days, half of them are somebody else's job, one is waiting on a trial balance that has not arrived, and the person who opens the screen on Friday is not the person who opened it on Tuesday. So the state is on the server, the progress is on the page, and any task can be opened in any order. Built as a wizard, the second person to touch it starts again at step 1 and the first person's work is invisible. Against settings-page: every setting on this screen lives in settings-page permanently, and that is where it is changed for the rest of the deployment's life. This page is a view over those same sections for the first month — it adds the order, the ownership, the dependencies and the progress, and nothing else. It is not a second home for a setting. The moment setup is complete it stops being a destination: the nav entry goes, the URL keeps working, and what is left is the record of who set what up and when. A checklist parked at 100% for three years is clutter with an audit trail attached, which is what the complete variant is about. Against import-page: several of these tasks are not forms at all — item masters, vendor masters and opening stock open the import screen — so this page links out to it and marks itself done from what the import posted. Do not rebuild an import here. And this is not a product tour: no coach marks, no tips, no dismissible overlay pointing at a button. A tour teaches an interface; this tracks work that people are already doing.
rules: It renders inside app-shell like every signed-in screen. The variants start at <main>; the shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark and the keyboard shortcuts, and the nav item that points here is the thing the complete variant takes away.

It is a checklist and not a wizard, and the whole markup follows from that. Every task is reachable at any time, nothing is behind a Next, and the state is server state on the company rather than per-user state in a browser. A checklist kept in localStorage tells the second person that nothing has been done, and the first person that it has, and neither of them finds out.

A blocked task is a link with a reason, never a disabled row. Disabled takes it out of the tab order, gives no reason and is the one control on the screen a keyboard cannot reach to be told why — and the reason is the only useful thing the row has. So the blocker is named in a sentence under the row, outside the row's own anchor so the link to it is a real link and not a link inside a link.

Two kinds of waiting, and they are not the same problem. A dependency is a fact the system knows and clears by itself — a lock mark in zinc-500, the neutral shade, because nothing is wrong. A person who has not answered is a state somebody set, so it carries a name, the date it was asked and the amber-700 warning mark, because it will not clear unless somebody chases it. Give both the same mark and the screen cannot tell you which of the six stalled tasks a phone call would fix.

Work time and waiting time are never added together. Two hours of typing and four days of waiting on a trial balance do not sum to anything anybody can plan against, so the header carries three separate figures — what you can start now, what is waiting on a person, what is waiting on a task — and the estimate on a row is only ever the typing.

A skipped task is not an unfinished one and the arithmetic has to show it. Seventeen tasks, two skipped, fifteen counted, nine done. The skipped ones keep their row, keep who skipped them and why, and can be brought back, which puts them back in the denominator. Print both figures or the progress bar becomes something to game.

Skipping asks for a reason and refuses to proceed without one. In November somebody asks why there are no customer masters, and "skipped" with no sentence beside it is indistinguishable from an oversight. The reason is short free text and it is shown wherever the skip is shown, including on the completion record.

Anything waiting on a skipped task is stranded and the screen says so. A skipped task never finishes, so a dependency on one never clears — that is the one place where skipping is not free, and it is the state the blocked variant spends a whole card on.

A task the server can detect is marked done from the fact, not from a tick. Item masters is done when the item table is not empty; opening stock is done when the first stock entry posts. A manual tick over a detectable fact goes stale the first time somebody deletes the rows again, and then the checklist is lying about the database it sits on.

Each task is its own URL with its own h1. Unlike import-page, where four stages are one document and the h1 must not change, a task here arrives in an email — "Meera has assigned you Approval limits" — and a page whose h1 says Set up Konspec has not told the person who opened that link what they are looking at.

A row that also carries a Mark done button cannot be one big link, because a form inside an anchor is not valid HTML and browsers repair it by moving the form out. Where the completion posts from the list, the row is a flex container with the title as the link and the form beside it; where it does not, the whole row is the link.

Every task shows who it is on, and unassigned is a state with its own block rather than an empty cell. The task nobody owns is the one that is still not done at go-live, and it is invisible in a list sorted by anything else.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, and let the phone variant's footer bar stick to the viewport.

anatomy.description: page-header's block: the one h1, and a line naming the company, the plants, the financial year and the go-live date everything on this screen is scoped to. No status pill — setup is not a record and none of the five locked statuses describes it.

A white card holding progress's bar over the counted total, the two figures written out, and the sentence that reconciles them with the number of tasks that exist. Its heading is what the bar is named by.

Three figures under the bar, never one: what can be started now with a time on it, what is waiting on a person, what is waiting on a task. Adding them together produces a number that describes nothing.
One named task at the foot of the summary card with the route into it, so the answer to "what do I do now" is on screen before any group is read.

card's shape, one per stage of the setup — company and plants, money and tax, master data, opening balances, people. An h2, one line saying what the group governs, the count done, and the task rows in a divided list.

marker's checklist item as a row: the state mark with its sr-only word, the task name, a meta line carrying who and when or who it is on, and the typing estimate on the right. The mark is the only colour on the row.
The sentence under a blocked row, outside the row's anchor, naming what it waits for as a real link and saying whether it clears by itself.
On optional tasks only, and absent rather than disabled on the rest. It opens a reason field in place and the reason is required; a skipped row afterwards carries who, when, why and Bring it back.

On the complete screen: the date this page leaves the navigation, what the URL becomes afterwards, the route to settings-page where the settings actually live, and a control for the person who wants it gone today.

behaviour: Any task can be opened at any time, including one that is blocked — the task page states the blocker and offers the route to it rather than refusing to render. Nothing on this screen enforces an order; the dependencies describe one.

A dependency clears itself. When the task it waits on is completed the blocked task becomes startable on the next render, with nobody going back to tick it, and the row's mark and sentence change together.

Marking a task done posts to the server and the progress figures, the bar and the group count are all rebuilt from the response. Nothing is kept in the browser, so a second person on a second machine sees the same page.
A task the server can detect is completed by the fact rather than by the button: the item import posting 1,240 rows finishes Item masters, and the button is not offered on those rows at all.

Skipping opens a reason field in place, requires it, and on success the row keeps its place in its group with the skipped mark, the reason and Bring it back. The denominator drops by one and the percentage is recomputed from the new one.
Reassigning a task is a change other people are told about — it appears in the resume variant's list of what happened while you were away, with who moved it and when.

The change list on the resume screen is measured from the user's last acknowledged visit, and that marker moves when they press Mark as read and at no other time. Moved on render, a three-second visit on a phone erases the record of four days somebody needed to read.

Below sm the group cards keep their rows and the estimate moves from the right of the row into the meta line. At 390px finished groups collapse to a single summary row and the next task moves out of the summary card into a bar pinned to the foot of the screen.

When the last counted task is done the page swaps to its completion state: the checklist becomes a record, the retirement date is set, and the navigation item is removed on that date rather than immediately, so the person who finished at 18:00 can still find it the next morning.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>. On the list screens it names the setup; on a task screen it names the task, because that is the page a link in an email lands on. Group cards are h2 and blocks inside a task are h3.

The progress bar is role="progressbar" on the track with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax counted in tasks rather than per cent, aria-labelledby pointing at the heading already on screen, and an aria-valuetext that says what the skipped tasks do to the figure. Read as "60%" it hides the two tasks that were taken out of the denominator.

Every state mark is an aria-hidden icon paired with an sr-only word at the front of the task name — Done, Blocked, Waiting on somebody, Skipped, Not started. Hiding the icon without putting the word back deletes the only carrier of the state, and leaving it audible reads out fifteen icon names down one list.

A blocked row is a real link and never disabled. The blocker sits in a paragraph after the row, outside its anchor, so the link to it is reachable — an anchor inside an anchor is repaired by the parser and the inner one stops existing.

The count of what is done is a role="status" that is in the document from first paint, so a completion or a skip writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message inside it is announced to nobody.

The skip reason field is a real labelled control, is focused when the panel opens, and its Cancel returns focus to the Skip button that opened it. Focus after a reveal needs a frame as well as a tick: at $nextTick the panel is still display:none and .focus() on it is a silent no-op.

Buttons that act on a named task carry the name in their accessible name — Send Nilesh Patil a reminder, Skip Opening customer balances — because Skip and Remind repeated down a screen name nothing, and a screen reader's control list is where they are read.
The avatar circle beside a person's name is aria-hidden, since the name is written beside it; otherwise it is announced as "NP Nilesh Patil".

The timeline of what changed while you were away is an ordered list, its rail and dots aria-hidden, and the dates carry the sequence in words. The rail is a picture of the order, not the record of it.

Nothing on this page is a coach mark, a tooltip on load or a focus trap. It is an ordinary document with links in it, which is what makes it survive being abandoned and reopened by somebody else four days later.

    Optional and done, which counts exactly like any other finished task. Optional describes whether it may be skipped, not how it is counted once it is not.

A skipped task is not an unfinished one

  • It leaves the denominator, so 9 of 15 rather than 9 of 17, and both figures stay on the page.
  • It never appears in what is next, and it never appears in the work-left estimate.
  • Anything waiting on it waits for ever. A skipped task never finishes, so the dependency never clears — that is the one cost, and it is why the screen names what is stranded.
  • It can be brought back at any time, which puts it into the denominator again and the count down with it.

What happens to this page
